text: No. Bats are [[mammal|mammals]], like cats, cows and people. They have fur, and mothers feed their babies milk. Birds have feathers and lay eggs. Bats and birds learned to fly separately, millions of years apart.

Bats are the only mammals that can flap and fly, rather than just glide. They are also very common. There are more than 1,400 kinds, about one in every five kinds of mammal on Earth. In India, big fruit bats called flying foxes hang in noisy groups from tall trees in many towns. At dusk they fly off to feed on fruit and flowers.

sec.t:
Most small bats hunt insects [[@nocturnal-animals|at night]]. They shout high-pitched calls, too high for our ears, and listen to the echoes that bounce back. This is called [[@echolocation|echolocation]]. It lets a bat find a moth in complete darkness and dodge thin branches.

Many big fruit bats do not echolocate at all. They find food with sharp eyes and a strong sense of smell. When a bat rests, it hangs upside down. Its toe tendons lock into place, so hanging takes almost no effort, even while it sleeps.

For their size, bats live a very long time. A mouse may live two years, but a small Brandt's bat in Siberia was found to be at least 41 years old. Most bats have just one baby, called a pup, each year. In crowded [[@caves-form|caves]], mothers find their own pup among thousands by its call and smell.

Bats face serious threats. In North America, a fungus disease called white-nose syndrome has killed millions of hibernating bats since it was first found in New York State in 2006. In India, old roosting trees are often cut down. Fruit bats can also carry some viruses, such as Nipah, which has caused outbreaks in Kerala. That is a good reason never to touch a bat, and to leave out fruit that an animal has nibbled.

Bats are good for people. Insect-eating bats gobble up huge numbers of [[@what-if-no-mosquitoes|mosquitoes]] and crop pests. Fruit bats drop seeds far from the parent tree, which helps forests spread. Bats pollinate the flowers of many plants, including wild [[@bananas|bananas]], and the agave plants of Mexico. In Southeast Asia, the smelly durian fruit depends largely on bats to carry its pollen.

In [[@texas|Texas]], Bracken Cave is home to millions of Mexican free-tailed bats every summer. When they pour out at sunset, the swirling cloud can be picked up on weather radar. In Austin, people gather on a city bridge on summer evenings just to watch more than a million bats leave for the night. To see how differently birds solve the same problem, read [[@how-birds-fly|how birds fly]].

text: We need insects because they keep the living world working. They pollinate many of the fruits, vegetables and nuts we eat. They break down dead plants, dead animals and dung, turning them back into [[@soil-made|soil]]. They are food for birds, frogs, fish, lizards and bats. Some even give us useful things such as honey, silk and lac.

Insects are also everywhere. About a million kinds have been named, more than all other animals put together, and there may be millions more still unknown. If [[@what-if-no-insects|insects disappeared]], many plants and animals, and the people who depend on them, would be in deep trouble.

st.reveal: Australia's native dung beetles were used to the dry droppings of kangaroos, not wet cow pats. Dung piled up, grass died under it and flies bred in it. Scientists brought in dozens of kinds of dung beetle that could bury cow dung, and many of them still work the fields today.

myth: Most insects are pests that harm people.

Only a small share of insect species bother people, damage crops or carry disease. Most are harmless to us, and many do jobs we depend on, such as pollinating crops, breaking down waste and feeding birds and fish.

sec.t:
Bees, butterflies, moths, flies and beetles carry pollen from flower to flower. That is how many plants make fruit and seeds. A major global report in 2016 found that more than three-quarters of the leading kinds of food crops benefit at least partly from animal [[@pollinators|pollinators]], most of them insects.

Mangoes, apples, coffee, cashews, chillies, cucumbers and cocoa all rely on insect visits to some degree. Insects also make food directly. Honeybees turn flower nectar into [[@honey|honey]], and in many countries [[@food-weird-world|people eat insects]] themselves. The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that about 2 billion people eat insects as part of their usual diet. In [[@odisha|Odisha]], a tangy chutney made from red weaver ants is a traditional dish around Similipal. In 2024 it received a GI tag, a label that protects foods and crafts linked to one region.

India has a long history with useful insects. [[@silk|Silk]] comes from the cocoons of silkworm caterpillars, and India makes several kinds, including mulberry, tussar, eri and golden muga silk from Assam.

Lac comes from tiny insects that live on trees such as kusum and palash. They give off a resin that people scrape off and turn into shellac, used for varnish, polish and traditional lac bangles. Jharkhand is one of India's biggest lac-producing states. Red dyes once came from insects too. Lac dye coloured cloth and leather in India for centuries, and cochineal, from a small bug living on cactus in Mexico, still colours some sweets and lipsticks today.

In 2017, a study from German nature reserves reported that the weight of flying insects caught in traps had fallen by about three-quarters over 27 years. Other studies have found declines in some places and little change in others. Scientists agree that habitat loss, pesticides, [[@night-sky-dark|light pollution]] and climate change all harm insects. They still debate how fast insects are declining worldwide, because careful long-term counts are rare.

Simple steps help: planting native flowers, leaving some wild corners and dead wood, and using fewer pesticides. Insects are small, but they make up a large share of animal life on land.

text: The blues is a kind of music created by African Americans in the Deep South of the United States, especially in the Mississippi Delta, in the late 1800s and early 1900s. It grew out of the work songs, field hollers and spirituals sung by enslaved people and their descendants, which carried musical ideas from West Africa.

A blues song is often about hard times: poverty, loneliness, lost love, unfair treatment or travelling far from home. It has a recognisable sound, with "blue" notes that bend between the usual pitches, a simple repeating chord pattern and a call-and-response feel. The blues became the root of [[@jazz|jazz]], rhythm and blues, [[@rock-music|rock and roll]] and much of the popular music heard today.

st.prompt: In many blues songs, how is a verse built?

options.t: A line is sung, repeated, then answered by a new line
Every line rhymes with the song's title
Each verse is sung by a different singer

st.reveal: A typical blues verse follows an A-A-B pattern. The singer states a line, sings it again, often with a twist, and then delivers a third line that answers or finishes the thought.

myth: The blues is always sad music.

Blues songs often deal with hard times, but many are funny, boastful, flirty or made for dancing. Singing about trouble was also a way of getting through it, and many listeners say the blues makes them feel better, not worse.

sec.t:
Enslaved Africans in America were forbidden many things, but they kept making music. Working in cotton fields, they sang together to keep time, share news and lift their spirits. One person would call out a line and the others would answer.

After [[@us-civil-war|slavery ended in 1865]], life for Black Americans in the South remained very hard, with unfair laws, low pay and violence. Field workers sang long, wavering "hollers" across the fields. Churches sang spirituals. From these sounds, a new style of song emerged, sung by one person with a guitar, harmonica or piano.

Many blues songs follow a pattern called the 12-bar blues: twelve short sections of music built on three chords, repeated again and again. The words often follow an A-A-B shape. The singer sings a line, repeats it, then answers with a new line.

The "blue notes" are what give the music its ache. Singers and guitarists bend certain notes slightly flat, between the keys on a piano. Listeners trained in Indian classical music sometimes hear something familiar in these sliding, in-between sounds.

In 1920, Mamie Smith recorded "Crazy Blues". It sold hugely, and record companies rushed to record Black singers. Women like Ma Rainey, called the "Mother of the Blues", and Bessie Smith became stars.

Between about 1910 and 1970, millions of Black Southerners moved north in what is called the Great Migration. Musicians went too. In [[@chicago|Chicago]], Muddy Waters plugged in an electric guitar and made the blues louder and tougher, so it could be heard in noisy clubs.

In the 1960s, young British musicians fell in love with American blues records. Bands such as the Rolling Stones, who named themselves after a Muddy Waters song, brought blues-based rock back to America. B.B. King toured the world for decades with his guitar, which he called Lucille. Today the blues is honoured with museums in Mississippi and Memphis, and its twelve bars sit underneath countless songs on the radio.

text: Nobody knows the name of the first painter, but we know where some of the oldest paintings are. On the island of Sulawesi in Indonesia, a cave wall shows three human-like figures beside a wild pig. Scientists have dated it to at least 51,200 years ago. It is the oldest known picture that tells a story.

Early artists ground coloured rocks into powder, mixed it with water or fat, and painted with fingers, chewed twigs or feathers. Some blew paint around a hand pressed on the wall, leaving a hand-shaped stencil that still says "I was here".
In India, the [[@art-cave-paintings-bhimbetka|rock shelters of Bhimbetka]] in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] hold thousands of paintings made over many thousands of years.

events.d: A painting of a wild pig and people, the oldest known picture that tells a story.
Lions, horses and rhinos painted by firelight, deep inside a cave.
Hundreds of rock shelters with hunters, dancers and animals painted in red and white.

Every drawing you make joins a story that began tens of thousands of years ago.

quiz.prompt: Red ochre paint has no carbon in it, so it can't be carbon-dated. How can scientists find the age of a red cave painting?

options.t: By dating the thin rock crust that grew over it
By counting the layers of dust on it
By testing how bright the red still is

quiz.reveal: Dripping water leaves thin crusts of a mineral called calcite on cave walls. Calcite traps a little uranium, which slowly turns into thorium at a known rate. If a crust formed on top of a painting, the painting must be older than the crust.

n.certNote: Dates for rock art are hard to measure. Some very old dates, including claims that Neanderthals made paintings, are still debated.

Lift your hand away and you will see its outline, just like the stencils left on cave walls tens of thousands of years ago.
myth: Cave people lived deep inside the caves they painted.
Most people lived in rock shelters, near cave entrances or in camps in the open. The deepest painted caves were dark, cold places that people visited, not homes.

sec.t:
Red and yellow came from [[ochre|ochre]], earth coloured by iron. Black came from charcoal from the fire, or from a dark mineral called manganese oxide. At Bhimbetka, white came from limestone.

These colours have lasted because they are made of [[mineral|minerals]], which don't rot. Many paintings also sat in sheltered spots, away from rain and strong sunlight. Paintings made out in the open have mostly washed away, so the pictures we can see today are a lucky sample. The painters of [[@ajanta-colours|Ajanta]], thousands of years later, still used many of the same earth colours.

sec.h: Bhimbetka, a gallery in the rocks
sec.t:
Bhimbetka's rock shelters sit in forested hills about 45 km from Bhopal. More than 700 shelters have been found in the area, and hundreds are painted. The pictures show hunters with bows, dancers holding hands, people [[@horses|riding horses]] and elephants, and animals such as bison, deer and [[@tiger-stripes|tigers]].

The oldest paintings may be around 10,000 years old, though exact dates are hard to pin down. Later artists painted over earlier ones, so a single wall can hold layers from many different times, rather like the stacked [[@history-sources|clues that historians use]]. The site became a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2003.

Many painted caves were discovered by accident. In 1957, the archaeologist V. S. Wakankar was travelling by train when he noticed rock formations near Bhimbetka. They reminded him of painted caves he had seen in Spain and France, so he went back to explore.

In 1940, four teenagers in south-west France squeezed down a hole in the ground and found Lascaux, a cave covered in painted horses, bulls and deer about 17,000 years old. So many visitors came afterwards that their breath and the lights began to damage the paintings. The cave was closed to the public in 1963, and visitors now see a careful copy built nearby.

Why did people paint at all? Nobody can ask them. Some experts link the pictures to hunting or ceremonies. Others think they simply told stories, long before anyone [[@writing-began|learned to write]].

text: Sayed Haider Raza was one of the most important Indian painters of the 20th century. He was born in 1922 in a village in the forests of Madhya Pradesh, trained in Nagpur and Bombay, and spent most of his life in France.

He is best known for the bindu, a dark circle placed at the centre of a painting with bright shapes and colours spreading out around it. These [[abstract|abstract]] works don't show people or places in the usual way. Instead they try to capture energy, nature and ideas from Indian philosophy. His paintings now hang in major museums and sell for crores of rupees.

A lotus flower
A face looking straight out

st.reveal: Raza called the bindu, or dot, a seed of energy from which everything grows. Around it he painted rings, triangles and bands of colour, which he linked to nature, the elements and Indian philosophy.

sec.h: A dot on the classroom wall
sec.t:
Raza grew up in Mandla district, near the [[@narmada|Narmada]] river, where his father was a forest officer. He later remembered dense jungles, dark nights and the fear and wonder they gave him.

He also remembered a teacher. Young Raza found it hard to concentrate, so the teacher drew a dot on the school wall and told him to stare at it. Raza said that exercise stayed with him all his life. Decades later, the same simple mark became the heart of his art.

He studied at the Nagpur School of Art and then at the Sir J.J. School of Art in Bombay. In his early years he painted watercolours of Bombay's streets and buildings.

In 1950, Raza won a scholarship to study in [[@paris|Paris]]. He stayed for about 60 years, married the French painter Janine Mongillat and lived partly in a village in southern France.

At first he painted French landscapes, with thick paint and stormy colours. Then, from the 1970s, something shifted. Raza began to look back toward India. He drew on the colours of Rajasthani miniatures and the black, red and yellow of Indian earth. He also read old Hindu and Buddhist ideas about how the world began.

Around 1980 the bindu arrived. He painted it again and again, surrounded by triangles, squares, rings and wavy lines. Titles were short and often Indian: *Bindu*, *Prakriti* (nature), *Germination*.

He usually worked in acrylic paint on canvas, building up flat, glowing areas of colour with clean edges. Some critics found the later works too repetitive. Admirers answer that no two are alike. Like a singer returning to a favourite raga, he kept changing the colours, the rhythm of the shapes and the mood around the same small circle.

Raza returned to live in India in 2010, at the age of 88, and kept painting in Delhi almost until his death in 2016. As he wished, he was buried in Mandla, next to his father.

In 2010, his painting *Saurashtra* sold at auction in London for about ₹16 crore. Raza used much of his wealth to set up the Raza Foundation, which gives grants to young artists, poets and dancers.

He received the Padma Vibhushan, one of India's highest civilian honours, in 2013, and France made him a member of its Legion of Honour in 2015. A painter from a forest village had found a language of shapes that people on both continents could feel.

text: Caste is an old system in South Asia that sorted people into groups by birth. For centuries, a person's caste often decided what work they could do, whom they could marry and even where they could draw water.

There are two ideas mixed together. The *varnas* were four broad classes described in ancient texts: priests, warriors, traders and labourers. The *jatis* are thousands of smaller, local communities, often linked to a trade. Below or outside them were people treated as "untouchable", who today mostly call themselves Dalits.
Since 1950, India's Constitution has banned discrimination by caste and abolished untouchability. Turning that law into everyday life has taken much longer.

st.reveal: The Chavdar tank in Mahad had been declared open to all, but Dalits were still kept away. Drinking its water was a simple act that claimed an equal right. It came three years before Gandhi's Salt March.

sec.t:
The four varnas appear in some of the oldest Hindu texts, from the [[@vedic-age|Vedic age]]. How strict the system was in practice changed from place to place and century to century. Some historians argue it was more flexible in the past. They say British rulers in the 1800s made it rigid by recording everyone's caste in the [[@census|census]] and using caste in laws and army recruitment. Others point to much older evidence of exclusion. Both views have serious scholars behind them.

Caste-like divisions are also found among some Muslim, Sikh and Christian communities in South Asia, even though their faiths teach equality.

B. R. Ambedkar was born in 1891 into a family treated as untouchable. As a schoolboy he had to sit apart and was not allowed to touch the water tap. He went on to earn doctorates from Columbia University in New York and the London School of Economics.

In 1927, he led the Mahad Satyagraha, where thousands drank from a public tank they had been barred from. Later, as chair of the committee that drafted [[@constitution|India's Constitution]], he made sure it outlawed untouchability and allowed special help for groups that had been kept down.

Ambedkar and Gandhi both opposed untouchability but disagreed on how to end it. Gandhi called Dalits *Harijan*, "people of God", a word many Dalits later rejected as patronising.

Laws passed in 1955 and 1989 made caste discrimination and violence punishable crimes. Reservation set aside seats in colleges, jobs and Parliament. In 1997, K. R. Narayanan became the first Dalit President of India. He had grown up in a poor family in Kerala and walked kilometres to school.

Cities have mixed people in schools, trains and offices in ways that would have been rare a century ago. Many young people now choose friends, and sometimes partners, without asking about caste. Yet [[@surveys|surveys]] still find that most marriages happen within the same caste, and cases of discrimination are reported every year. The fight Ambedkar started is still going on.

text: Cities compete to host the Olympics, the football World Cup and other giant events because they hope to gain fame, tourists and new buildings. A big event puts a city on television screens around the world for weeks. Governments often use the deadline to build metro lines, airports and roads that might otherwise take decades.

But hosting is enormously expensive. Stadiums, athletes' villages, security and transport can cost billions of dollars, and studies show the costs almost always end up higher than planned. Whether it is worth it depends a lot on how the city plans, and on what it does with everything afterwards.

st.prompt: Researchers at Oxford University studied the costs of Olympic Games since 1960. How many came in on or under budget?

About half
Almost all

st.reveal: The Oxford studies found that every Games with reliable data went over budget, often by a large amount. Building giant venues on a fixed deadline, with no option to delay, makes overspending very likely.

myth: Hosting the Olympics always makes a city richer.

Some hosts gained new transport and a better image, but many spent far more than they earned. Studies of the Games since 1960 found that every one with good data went over budget, and some left empty stadiums behind.

sec.t:
Montreal spent so much on the 1976 Olympics that the province of Quebec took about 30 years to pay off the debt, finishing in 2006. Its stadium's tower and roof ran years late. Many venues from the 2004 Athens Games sat empty and crumbling for years afterwards. Football's [[@fifa-world-cup|World Cup]] has the same problem. For the 2014 tournament, Brazil built a large stadium in Manaus, deep in the Amazon, for just four group matches. The city's own clubs rarely draw crowds anywhere near big enough to fill it.

The 2010 Delhi Commonwealth Games were hit by delays, cost overruns and corruption charges against officials, which embarrassed the country. Studies led by Bent Flyvbjerg at Oxford University found that every Olympics since 1960 for which data exist went over budget. Fixed deadlines are part of the problem: a stadium cannot be delayed for a year when the opening ceremony date is already set.

Los Angeles took another path in 1984. Few other cities wanted the Games after Montreal's troubles, so LA could set its own terms. It used existing stadiums, including the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, the main stadium of the 1932 Olympics, and paid for the rest with corporate sponsors and TV money. The Games ended with a surplus of over 200 million dollars.

LA plans to repeat the idea for 2028, using venues that already exist. The International Olympic Committee now encourages cities to reuse buildings and spread events across a region, partly because fewer cities have been willing to bid.

India hopes to host a Summer Olympics, and in 2024 it formally told the International Olympic Committee it was interested in the 2036 Games. Meanwhile, [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]] has been named as the host of the 2030 Commonwealth Games. Supporters say big events could build sports facilities, inspire young athletes and boost tourism. Sceptics warn about costs and ask whether the money would do more good spent on schools, hospitals and local playgrounds.

Good [[@urban-planning|urban planning]] may matter more than the event itself. A stadium used every week by local clubs, or a metro line still crowded twenty years later, is the kind of legacy that makes the cost easier to defend.

text: Life in a fishing village runs on the sea's timetable. Boats often leave in the dark, long before sunrise, and come back in the early morning with their catch. By the time the sun is fully up, the beach becomes a busy market, with fish laid out in rows and auctions shouted at top speed.

India has thousands of fishing villages along its coastline of about 11,000 km. Fishing feeds millions of families and brings fish to plates far inland. But it is hard work, it depends on weather and seasons, and it is changing fast.

st.prompt: Why do Indian states stop most fishing at sea for about two months each year?

options.t: To give fish time to breed, during the stormy monsoon
Because the sea freezes
Because there are festival holidays

st.reveal: Many fish breed around the monsoon months, and the sea is also at its roughest then. The ban protects both the young fish and the fishers.

sec.t:
Many fishers set out around 3 or 4 in the morning. Some use small wooden boats or catamarans close to shore. Others go out on motor trawlers for days at a time. Fishers read the wind, the colour of the water, the birds diving overhead and the phase of the moon to guess where fish will be.

Back on land, the work keeps going. Nets are untangled and mended by hand, often by older men who sit in the shade with a wooden needle. Mending a big net can take days. Children grow up knowing how to tie dozens of knots before they can ride a bicycle. Most nets today are made of nylon, which lasts much longer than the cotton and coir nets of the past.

sec.t:
Every year, Indian states ban most fishing at sea for about two months. On the west coast, it usually runs from 1 June to 31 July. On the east coast, it falls in April to June. This gives fish time to breed, and keeps boats safe from stormy [[@monsoon|monsoon]] seas.

Fishers spend the break repairing boats and nets, and many take other jobs. Families save money in the good months to get through the lean ones. Fishing communities also have their own festivals. On Narali Purnima, the Kolis offer coconuts to the sea to mark the end of the monsoon and the start of the new fishing season.

India produces more fish than almost any other country. It ranks second in the world, with around 8% of the global total in recent years, counting fish from both sea and farms. Seafood from India's coast is exported to the USA, Europe and Asia.

But the sea is under pressure. Big trawlers catch huge amounts, and some kinds of fish are getting harder to find. Rising seas and stronger storms threaten beachside homes. Some villages now plant [[@mangroves|mangroves]], whose tangled roots protect the shore and shelter baby fish.

Fishing villages exist on every coast. In Gloucester, Massachusetts, one of the oldest fishing ports in the USA, a famous bronze statue of a fisherman at the wheel remembers those lost at sea. In Kochi, giant cantilevered fishing nets dip into the water like huge spiders, and the question of who brought them to [[@kochi|Kochi]] is still debated. And every fishing village lives by the [[@tides|tides]], the Moon's twice-a-day tug on the ocean.

text: A supreme court is the highest court in a country. Its decisions are final: there is nowhere higher to appeal. Lower courts across the country must follow its rulings.

Its biggest job is to protect the constitution. If a government action or a law goes against it, the supreme court can cancel it. Supreme courts also settle disputes between states, and between citizens and the government.

India's Supreme Court sits in New Delhi and started work in 1950. The US Supreme Court sits in Washington, D.C., and first met in 1790. Both are watched closely, because their decisions can change how millions of people live.

sec.t:
The [[@constitution|Constitution of India]] gives every citizen fundamental rights, such as equality and [[@free-speech|freedom of speech]]. Article 32 lets anyone go straight to the Supreme Court if those rights are broken. Dr B.R. [[@ambedkar|Ambedkar]] called this article "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it".

In the USA, the court gave itself a similar power in 1803, in a case called *Marbury v. Madison*. It ruled that judges can strike down laws that conflict with the [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]]. This power is called judicial review.

In 1954, in *Brown v. Board of Education*, the US Supreme Court ruled that keeping Black and white children in separate public schools broke the Constitution. All nine justices agreed. It was a turning point for the American [[@civil-rights|civil rights]] movement, though many schools resisted for years.

In the late 1970s and 1980s, Indian judges noticed that the poorest people almost never reached the Supreme Court. Lawyers cost too much. So judges like P.N. Bhagwati began treating letters about injustice as petitions. This grew into public interest litigation, which lets anyone go to court on behalf of people who can't.

Cases about prisoners, bonded labourers and polluted rivers reached the court this way. Critics say the court sometimes goes too far into decisions better left to governments, a debate that continues.

India's Supreme Court can have up to 34 judges, who retire at 65. They usually hear cases in small groups called benches. Senior judges have a big say in choosing new ones, through a group called the collegium. The court has a huge backlog, with tens of thousands of cases waiting.

The US court has nine justices, who serve for life. The president nominates them and the Senate must approve. They hear only around 60 cases a year, chosen from thousands of requests.

For centuries, Lady Justice has been shown blindfolded, holding scales and a sword. In 2024, a new statue in India's Supreme Court library showed her with open eyes, holding the Constitution instead of a sword. News reports said the change was meant to show that the law is not blind, and that justice in India rests on the Constitution.

text: The oldest board games we know of are about 4,500 to 5,000 years old. Senet, from ancient Egypt, and the Royal Game of Ur, from [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], in present-day Iraq, are among the oldest whose boards survive. Both are race games, where players roll dice-like pieces and move counters along a track.

Other ancient games include Go, from China, and mancala games, where seeds or stones are moved between pits. India gave the world chaturanga, [[@pop-chess-pieces|the ancestor of chess]], and pachisi, the ancestor of [[@ludo|Ludo]].

st.reveal: Irving Finkel of the British Museum translated a clay tablet from 177 BCE that described how to play. The game had survived for over 2,000 years by then. A version was even still played in Kochi, in Kerala, in the 20th century.

sec.t:
Senet boards have 30 squares in three rows. Players threw casting sticks, like flat dice, and moved pieces along the board. Pictures in tombs show Egyptians playing it more than 4,500 years ago.

Over time Senet took on religious meaning, as a symbol of the soul's journey after death. Several Senet boards were buried with Tutankhamun so he could play in the afterlife. We still do not know the exact rules of [[@ancient-egypt|ancient Egypt's]] favourite game. Modern versions are educated guesses.

Archaeologists have found dice and what may be gaming pieces at [[@indus-cities|Indus Valley]] sites such as Mohenjo-daro, about 4,500 years old. Dice games appear in the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]], where Yudhishthira loses his kingdom in a game of dice.

Pachisi, played on a cross-shaped board, was a royal favourite. At Fatehpur Sikri, there is a large board marked out in the paving of a courtyard. Stories say [[@akbar|Akbar]] played there with people as pieces. Chaturanga, a war game with [[@oddity-elephants-war|elephants]], horses, [[@wheel-to-chariot|chariots]] and foot soldiers, grew into [[@chess-india|chess]]. Gyan chaupar became [[@snakes-ladders|Snakes and Ladders]].

Go, called weiqi in China and baduk in Korea, is played with black and white stones on a grid of 19 by 19 lines. It is at least 2,500 years old and its rules are simple, yet it is one of the hardest games in the world to master. In 2016 a computer program, AlphaGo, beat one of the world's best players.

Mancala games are played across Africa and Asia. In south India, a version called pallanguzhi uses a wooden board with 14 pits and cowrie shells or seeds.

Board games survive because they need little more than a board and some pieces, yet each game is different. Many mix luck and skill, so a beginner can win sometimes. Children and grandparents can play together.

Modern hits like Monopoly, first sold in 1935, are based on earlier games too. Monopoly grew from The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 by Lizzie Magie. When you play Ludo on a phone today, you are playing a game that Indian royalty knew centuries ago.

text: The Tour de France is the most famous bicycle race in the world. Every July, about 22 teams of riders race around France, and sometimes into neighbouring countries, for three weeks. The race is split into 21 day-long stages, with two rest days. Altogether riders cover roughly 3,300 to 3,500 kilometres, including long climbs in the Alps and the Pyrenees.

Each rider's times are added up. The rider with the lowest total time wears the yellow jersey, the maillot jaune, and whoever holds it at the end wins. The race usually finishes on the Champs-Élysées in [[@paris|Paris]].

st.reveal: Riding behind another cyclist, called drafting, saves a lot of energy because the rider in front pushes the air aside. In a big group, called the peloton, riders in the middle can use far less effort than one rider out in front alone.

d.try: On a windy day, walk into the wind holding a large piece of cardboard flat in front of you, then turn it sideways. Feel how much harder the flat side pushes back. Cyclists crouch low and ride in groups to cut down that push from the air.
myth: The rider who wins the most stages wins the Tour.

The overall winner is the rider with the lowest total time across all stages. A rider can win the Tour without winning a single stage, and fast sprinters can win several stages without coming close overall.

sec.t:
The Tour was invented in 1903 by a French sports newspaper, *L'Auto*, to beat a rival paper. Its editor, Henri Desgrange, hoped readers would buy the paper every day to follow the riders. It worked.

Early riders rode heavy bikes with no [[@gears|gears]] on rough, unlit roads, sometimes through the night. Some cheated by catching trains. In 1919 the leader was given a yellow jersey, matching the colour of [[@newspapers|*L'Auto*'s pages]], so spectators could spot him.

The main group of riders is called the [[peloton|peloton]]. Inside it, riders save energy because those in front block the wind. This is called drafting. A rider sheltered in the middle may use much less effort than one alone at the front.

That is why riders who break away often get caught before the finish. Pushing alone against the air, a form of [[@friction|friction]] called drag, wears them out. Teams take turns at the front, then drop back to rest.

The route changes every year and is announced each October. Some years the race starts in another country. The 2024 Tour began in Italy and, because Paris was busy with the Olympics, finished in Nice instead. Millions of people line the roads for free, and some camp on mountain passes for days to get a good spot.

Mountain stages are the hardest. The climb up Alpe d'Huez has 21 hairpin bends. Mont Ventoux is a bare, windy mountain in Provence. Some passes in the Alps rise above 2,000 metres, higher than Ben Nevis, Britain's tallest peak, at 1,345 metres.

Riders can burn about 5,000 to 6,000 kilocalories on a mountain day, more than twice what most adults eat. They eat rice cakes, gels and energy bars while riding, grabbing bags of food from helpers at the roadside.

Five riders have won the Tour five times: Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault, Miguel Induráin and, in 2026, Tadej Pogačar of Slovenia. The American Lance Armstrong won seven times, but all seven titles were taken away in 2012 after it was proved he had used banned drugs. Cheating with drugs, called [[doping|doping]], damaged the race badly for years.

In 1989 another American, Greg LeMond, won by just 8 seconds after 3,285 kilometres, the closest finish ever. In recent years Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard of Denmark have battled for the yellow jersey. A women's Tour de France Femmes began in 2022.

text: Halloween is celebrated on 31 October, mainly in the USA, [[@canada|Canada]], the UK and Ireland, and more and more in other countries, including India. Children dress up in costumes, carve pumpkins and go from house to house saying "trick or treat" to collect sweets.

Its roots go back a long way. Many historians link it to Samhain, an ancient festival of the Celtic peoples of Ireland, [[@scotland|Scotland]] and nearby lands. Later, it mixed with the Christian feast of All Saints. Irish and Scottish immigrants carried the customs to America, where Halloween grew into the festival known today.

sec.h: Samhain and the dark half of the year
sec.t:
For the Celts, Samhain, held around 1 November, marked the end of the harvest and the start of winter, the dark half of the year. As [[@seasons-why|the seasons]] turned, nights grew long and cold.

According to old stories, Samhain was a time when the boundary between the living and the dead grew thin. People lit bonfires, and some may have worn disguises so wandering spirits would not recognise them. Because few written records survive from those times, historians are careful about how much they claim.

In Ireland and Scotland, people carved faces into turnips and other root vegetables and put a coal or candle inside. A folk tale told of "Stingy Jack", a man who tricked the devil and was doomed to wander with only a glowing coal in a turnip.

In the 1800s, large numbers of Irish people came to the USA, especially after the famine of the 1840s. They found pumpkins, which grow well in North America and are much easier to carve. The pumpkin jack-o'-lantern was born.

The phrase "trick or treat" became common in North America in the 1930s. After the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], as sweets became cheaper and suburbs spread, trick-or-treating became a huge event for American children. Today Americans spend billions of dollars on Halloween sweets, costumes and decorations each year.

Halloween also sits in a season of festivals about the dead around the world. In [[@mexico|Mexico]], the Day of the Dead, on 1 and 2 November, honours family members who have died with marigolds and photographs. It's a separate festival, with its own roots, but it falls at the same time of year.

sec.h: Why being scared can be fun
sec.t:
Halloween is full of ghosts, skeletons, witches and [[@bats-fly|bats]], though real bats are harmless insect-eaters. Many people enjoy a little fright when they know they are safe. Scientists say a short scare makes the heart beat faster, then floods us with relief, which can feel exciting.

In Indian cities, Halloween parties have become popular in schools and malls. India also has its own times for remembering ancestors, such as Pitru Paksha, a fortnight in which many Hindu families offer food and prayers to those who have died.

text: No, not in the simple way the popular idea suggests. Your brain does have two halves, called [[hemisphere|hemispheres]], and they are not identical. In most people, the left hemisphere does more of the work of language, and the right does more of the work of recognising faces and judging space.

But maths isn't a left-brain job, and art isn't a right-brain one. Both use many areas spread across both sides, connected by a thick bridge of nerve fibres. And no one is "left-brained" or "right-brained". Everyone uses their whole brain.

st.reveal: Maths draws on many regions in both hemispheres. Some help with number sense, some with words, some with picturing shapes, and some with memory. Art and music also use both halves.

sec.t:
Look at a model of the brain and you'll see a deep groove running front to back, dividing it into left and right. Each half controls movement and feeling on the opposite side of the body. If you wave your right hand, signals mostly come from your left hemisphere.

The two halves talk constantly through the corpus callosum, a band of roughly 200 million nerve fibres. Information flashes across it in a fraction of a second, so the two sides work as one team. Our article on [[@brain-works|how the brain works]] explains how [[neuron|neurons]] pass these messages.

In 1861, a French doctor named Paul Broca examined a patient who could understand speech but could say almost nothing except one syllable, "tan". After the man died, Broca found damage in a small area on the left side of his brain. Other patients showed the same pattern.

This was early evidence that, for most people, key language areas sit in the left hemisphere. Today we know this is true for about 95 percent of right-handed people and most left-handed people too.

Newspapers, magazines and self-help books took these careful findings and stretched them. Soon people were told the left brain was logical and the right brain creative, and that each person had a "dominant" side that shaped their personality.

In 2013, scientists at the University of Utah looked at brain scans from over 1,000 people. They found that particular networks did lean to one side, but individuals didn't use one hemisphere more than the other overall. Nobody was left-brained or right-brained. It is a good example of [[@statistics-lies|how a real finding can be stretched]] into a false story.

About one person in ten is [[@left-handed|left-handed]]. [[@leonardo|Leonardo da Vinci]], for instance, wrote his notes from right to left in [[@mirrors|mirror]] writing. Left-handers are a little more likely than right-handers to have language spread over both hemispheres, or mainly on the right. But being left-handed doesn't make someone more artistic, and being right-handed doesn't make someone better at maths.

Brains are also flexible. When a young child's brain is injured on one side, the other side can often take over jobs like language. Your [[@memory|memory]], your maths and your music all live in networks that stretch across both halves of your head.

text: A reflex is an action your body does on its own, without you deciding to. When you blink at a speck of dust, sneeze at pepper or yank your hand off a hot pan, a reflex is at work.

Many reflexes take a shortcut. A [[nerve|nerve]] in your skin senses danger and sends a signal to your spinal cord, the thick cable of nerves running down your back. Instead of waiting for the brain, the spinal cord sends a message straight back out to your [[@muscles|muscles]]. This loop is called a reflex arc. Because the signal travels a shorter path, [[@sport-science-reaction-time|the reaction is very fast]]. Your brain finds out a moment later.

st.reveal: The signal from your hand reaches your spinal cord, which sends a message straight back to your arm muscles. Your hand starts moving before the pain message has finished reaching your brain. You feel the burn a moment after you've already moved.

sec.t:
Doctors often test reflexes by tapping just below the knee with a small rubber hammer. The tap stretches a tendon, which tells the thigh muscle it's being pulled. The spinal cord answers by tightening the muscle, and your lower leg kicks forward.

This knee-jerk reflex normally helps you keep your balance. If your knee starts to buckle while you're standing, the same loop tightens the muscle and keeps you upright. If the kick is much too weak or much too strong, it can tell a doctor something about how the nerves are working.

Newborn babies have some reflexes that older children don't. Stroke a newborn's palm, and their fingers curl tightly around yours. Touch their cheek, and they turn their head and open their mouth, searching for milk. A sudden noise makes them fling their arms out and then pull them in, which is the startle reflex.

These fade over the first months as the [[@brain-works|brain]] takes more control. Doctors check them at a baby's health check-ups because they show the [[@nervous-system|nervous system]] is developing well. The grasp reflex may be left over from our primate relatives, whose babies cling to their mother's fur.

Some fast moves aren't reflexes at all. A cricket ball bowled at 150 km/h travels about 20 metres from the bowler's hand to the batter. Using [[@speed-distance|speed and distance]], that's under half a second. A batter has to see it, judge its line and [[@cricket-swing|swing]], and decide on a shot, then move.

That's a reaction, not a reflex, because the brain has to choose. Most people take about a fifth of a second just to react to something they see. Top batters and baseball hitters manage because years of practice let them read the bowler's arm and grip early and guess where the ball will go. A simple reflex, like the knee jerk, can be several times faster than that.

text: Marie Curie was a Polish-born scientist who worked in France. With her husband Pierre, she discovered two new chemical elements, polonium and radium, in 1898. She also gave a name to the strange energy that some materials give off on their own: [[radioactive|radioactivity]].

She was the first woman to win a [[@accident-dynamite|Nobel Prize]], and she won a second one eight years later. Her work changed how scientists think about the atom and led to new ways of treating cancer. It also slowly harmed her health, because nobody yet knew how dangerous radiation could be.

sec.t:
Curie was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw in 1867. Poland was then ruled by [[@russia|Russia]], and Polish universities did not accept women. Maria and her sister Bronisława studied at the "Flying University", a secret school that moved from house to house to avoid the authorities.

The sisters made a deal. Maria worked as a governess and sent money to help Bronisława study medicine in [[@paris|Paris]]. Then Bronisława helped Maria. In 1891, aged 24, Maria arrived at the Sorbonne. She was so poor that she sometimes fainted from [[@hunger|hunger]] while studying, but she finished first in her class in physics.

In Paris she met Pierre Curie, a physicist, and they married in 1895. The next year, Henri Becquerel found that [[@accident-radioactivity|uranium gave off invisible rays]]. Marie decided to study them for her doctorate.

She noticed that a uranium ore called pitchblende was far more active than its uranium alone could explain. Something else must be hiding inside. The Curies worked in a leaky old shed, grinding and boiling tonnes of ore. In 1898 they announced polonium, named after Poland, and then radium, which glowed faintly blue in the dark. It took them almost four more years of hard labour to collect a tenth of a gram of pure radium salt. That is about the weight of a few grains of rice, but it proved radium was real.

In 1903 the Curies and Becquerel shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1906, Pierre was killed in a street accident in Paris. Marie took over his job and became the first woman professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own.

{{story:world-war-one}}

sec.h: Little Curies on the front line
sec.t:
When the [[@world-war-one|First World War]] began in 1914, Curie realised that [[@x-rays|X-ray]] machines could help surgeons find bullets and broken bones in wounded soldiers. She helped equip about 20 cars with X-ray machines and power generators. Soldiers called them "petites Curies", little Curies. She learned to drive and often operated the machines herself, with her teenage daughter Irène.

Around 200 more X-ray rooms were set up in field hospitals. Historians estimate that over a million wounded soldiers were X-rayed.

The Curies carried test tubes of radium in their pockets and kept them in desk drawers. They had no idea how harmful radiation was. Marie Curie died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, a blood disease almost certainly caused by years of exposure.

Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie went on to share the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with her husband. In 1995, Marie and Pierre's remains were moved to the Panthéon in Paris. She was the first woman honoured there for her own achievements. Her papers are still radioactive, because radium has a [[@half-life|half-life]] of about 1,600 years.

text: Machu Picchu is a stone city built on a narrow ridge high in the Andes mountains of [[@peru|Peru]], about 2,430 metres above sea level. The Incas built it around 1450, most likely as a royal estate for their emperor Pachacuti.

Inca builders used the granite of the mountain itself. With stone and bronze tools, they shaped blocks so precisely that they fit together without mortar, which is the cement-like paste that normally holds bricks together. They built terraces down the steep slopes, laid hidden drainage under the city, and designed walls that rock gently during [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]] instead of falling down. Most of the work was done by teams of labourers who owed work to the state as a kind of tax.

st.prompt: The Incas had no writing system like ours. How did they keep records of taxes and people?

With paintings on cave walls

st.reveal: A quipu was a main cord with many hanging strings. The type, position and number of knots stood for numbers, using a base-ten system. Trained record-keepers could read them to track harvests, taxes and censuses.

n.certNote: Most archaeologists agree Machu Picchu was a royal estate built for the emperor Pachacuti around 1450. Exactly how it was used, and how long people lived there, is still studied.

myth: Hiram Bingham discovered Machu Picchu in 1911.
Local farmers knew the site well and led him to it, and some families were growing crops on its terraces. Bingham's photographs and articles made it famous around the world.

sec.t:
The Incas built the largest empire in the Americas. At its height around 1500, it stretched about 4,000 km along the Andes, through today's Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina. Its capital was Cusco.

They had no horses, no iron and no wheeled carts. Yet they ruled millions of people. A road network of about 30,000 km, with rope [[@bridges|bridges]] across gorges, linked the empire. Relay runners called *chasquis* carried messages along it, covering great distances in a few days.

sec.h: Stones that fit like puzzle pieces

sec.t:
The ridge is steep and wet, with heavy rains for part of the year. A city here could easily slide away. So builders put much of their effort below ground, into foundations and layers of crushed rock that let rainwater drain away.

The terraces on the slopes held soil in place and gave farmland. Llamas, relatives of [[@camels|camels]], carried loads up and down, though each one can only carry about 25 to 30 kg. Most of the heavy lifting was done by people, with ropes, ramps and levers.

About a century after it was built, Machu Picchu was abandoned, around the time Spanish soldiers led by [[@spanish-conquest|Francisco Pizarro]] conquered the Incas in the 1530s. The Spanish destroyed or rebuilt many Inca sites, but there is no sign they ever reached Machu Picchu.

Local farmers knew it was there. In 1911, a farmer named Melchor Arteaga led the American explorer Hiram Bingham up the mountain. Bingham's photographs in *National Geographic* made it world-famous. He also shipped thousands of objects to Yale University in the USA, which returned them to Peru from 2011 onwards.

Machu Picchu became a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site in 1983 and is one of the most visited places in South America. In 2007 it was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

Peru now limits visitor numbers to protect the site. Many people still walk the Inca Trail there over several days, following old stone paths. The Incas also domesticated the [[@potatoes|potato]] in these mountains, a crop that eventually reached Indian kitchens as the humble aloo.

text: Canada is a huge country in the north of North America, stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific and up into the Arctic. It has endless forests, cold blue lakes, prairies of wheat, towering mountains and frozen islands near the North Pole.

For all that space, only about 4 crore people live there. Most of them crowd into a narrow band in the south, close to the border with the United States, where the weather is gentlest. Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver are the biggest cities. The capital is Ottawa, not Toronto, which surprises many visitors.

st.reveal: Canada's coast, with its thousands of Arctic islands, stretches roughly 2,40,000 km. India's is about 11,000 km by the latest official count. Australia's is long too, but nowhere near Canada's.

Almost no one lives in an igloo. Inuit hunters traditionally built them as quick shelters on hunting trips. Southern cities like Toronto have hot, humid summers, often reaching 30 °C.

sec.h: Lakes, forests and a lot of cold
sec.t:
Canada has more lakes than any other country. Some, like [[@great-lakes|Lake Superior]], which it shares with the US, are so big that they have waves and shipwrecks. Forests cover over a third of the land, and much of the far north sits on [[permafrost|permafrost]], ground that stays frozen all year.

Winters can be fierce. In 1947 a village called Snag, in the Yukon, recorded about minus 63 °C, [[@weather-records|the coldest temperature]] ever measured in North America outside Greenland. Up north, people often see the [[@aurora|northern lights]] ripple green and purple across the night sky. Yet in summer, the same country has sunny beaches and fruit farms.

The wild animals match the landscape. Moose wade into lakes to eat water plants, black bears raid berry bushes, and polar bears wait on the shores of Hudson Bay for the sea to freeze. In the town of Churchill, Manitoba, so many polar bears pass through each autumn that many people don't lock their car doors, so anyone surprised by a bear can jump inside.

Nearly one in four people in Canada was born in another country. Large numbers come from India, China and the Philippines. [[@punjabi-gurmukhi|Punjabi]] is one of the most spoken languages in Canada after English and French, and cities like Brampton and Surrey have big Indian communities, with gurdwaras, sweet shops and [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]] fireworks.

Families move for jobs, study and to join relatives. Their stories are part of a wider pattern you can read about in [[@immigration-stories|immigration stories]]. Many Indian students now study at Canadian universities too.

sec.h: Hockey, basketball and a maple leaf
sec.t:
Ice hockey is the sport Canadians love most, played on frozen ponds and rinks from childhood. Less well known is that a Canadian, James Naismith, invented [[@basketball|basketball]] in 1891, while teaching at a college in Massachusetts. His first hoops were peach baskets nailed to a balcony.

The red maple leaf on Canada's flag has been there since 1965. Maple trees give maple syrup, made by boiling down the sweet sap that flows in early spring. It takes roughly 40 litres of sap to make 1 litre of syrup, so a bottle on a pancake table represents a lot of patient boiling.

text: Jaipur is the capital of Rajasthan. Its old walled city is painted a warm pinkish terracotta. In 1876, Maharaja Ram Singh II had the buildings painted to welcome the Prince of Wales from Britain, and pink was seen as a colour of hospitality. A writer later called Jaipur the Pink City, and the name stuck.
Shopfronts in the old city are still painted the same shade, so the bazaars look much as they did 150 years ago. Today over 30 lakh people live in Jaipur.

st.prompt: Why was Jaipur's old city painted pink in 1876?

options.t: To welcome a visiting British prince
Because pink paint keeps buildings cooler
To mark the birth of a royal baby

st.reveal: Maharaja Ram Singh II had the city painted for the visit of the Prince of Wales, later King Edward VII. Pink was seen as a colour of welcome. Shops in the old city are still painted the same shade today.

d.try: Make a shadow clock. On a sunny morning, stand a pencil upright in a lump of clay on a sheet of paper in a sunny spot that won't be moved. Every hour, mark the end of the shadow and write the time. By afternoon you will have a simple sundial, like a tiny Samrat Yantra.
myth: Jaipur's Hawa Mahal is a huge palace with hundreds of rooms.
It is mostly a tall, thin screen wall at the edge of the City Palace, only one room deep in places. Its many small windows let royal women watch the street below without being seen.

sec.t:
Jaipur was one of the first planned cities in India. In 1727, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II decided to move his capital down from the hilltop fort of Amber. With the architect Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, he laid the city out in a grid of large blocks, with wide straight streets meeting at right angles.

The plan followed ideas from old Indian texts on building, called Vastu Shastra and Shilpa Shastra. Each block had its own purpose, from markets to palaces. Even now you can walk straight down the bazaars and see the [[@symmetry|symmetry]] of the arches and shopfronts on both sides.

The Hawa Mahal, built in 1799, is Jaipur's most famous sight. Its pink sandstone face rises five storeys and is covered in small windows called jharokhas, often counted at 953. Breezes blowing through them kept the rooms cool, which is how it got its name: Palace of Winds.

Royal women followed purdah, a custom of staying out of public view. The windows let them watch festivals and processions in the street below without being seen. The building is mostly a screen, very thin compared with its height.

Jaipur is ringed by hills topped with forts. Amber Fort, the old capital, is built of pale yellow and pink sandstone and white marble. Its Sheesh Mahal, or mirror palace, has walls covered in tiny pieces of mirror that sparkle when a single candle is lit. Nahargarh and Jaigarh forts stand on the ridges above, and Jaigarh holds a huge cannon called Jaivana. A long wall with watchtowers runs along the hills between the forts, a little like a small [[@great-wall|Great Wall]]. From the top you can see why the kings chose this valley: hills on most sides made it easy to guard, and lakes stored the precious rain.

Jaipur is famous for crafts. Nearby villages such as Sanganer and Bagru are known for [[@block-printing|block printing]], where carved wooden blocks stamp patterns onto cloth. The city is also a centre for cutting [[@gems-crystals|gemstones]] and for [[@blue-pottery|blue pottery]]. [[@kite-flying|Kite flying]] fills the sky on Makar Sankranti in January. In 2019, UNESCO named the walled city of Jaipur a World Heritage Site, two years after Ahmedabad became India's first World Heritage City.

text: Spanish spread mostly through empire. Starting in 1492, Spain sent ships, soldiers, priests and settlers across the Atlantic. Over the next three centuries, it ruled most of South America, Central America, Mexico, much of the Caribbean and large parts of what is now the USA. It also ruled the Philippines in Asia.

Spanish became the language of government, church, schools and trade in all those places. When the colonies became independent countries in the 1800s, they kept the language. Today Spanish is an official language in about 20 countries and is spoken as a first language by about 500 million people, more than any other language except Mandarin Chinese.

st.reveal: In 1494, Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, dividing newly found lands between them. Portugal got the eastern bulge of South America, which became Brazil. That is why Brazilians speak Portuguese while almost all their neighbours speak Spanish.

sec.h: From Roman soldiers to Spanish kings
sec.t:
Spanish began as the everyday Latin spoken by people in Roman Spain. After the Roman Empire fell, that Latin slowly changed into several local languages, including Castilian, from the kingdom of Castile in central Spain. Castilian is what most people now call Spanish.

From 711, much of Spain was ruled by Muslim kingdoms, a region known as al-Andalus, for nearly 800 years in some places. Arabic left thousands of words in Spanish, from *aceite* (olive oil) to *almohada* (pillow). Many words starting with "al-" come from the Arabic word for "the".

In 1492, the last of these kingdoms, Granada, fell to the Spanish monarchs. In the same year, they paid for [[@columbus|Columbus]] to sail west. That same year, a scholar named Antonio de Nebrija published one of the first grammar books of Spanish, and he told the queen that language had always been a companion of empire.

{{story:columbus}}

sec.h: An empire, and what it cost
sec.t:
[[@spanish-conquest|Spanish conquerors]] defeated the [[@aztecs-maya|Aztec and Inca empires]] in the 1500s. Diseases brought from Europe, such as [[@disease-history|smallpox]], killed huge numbers of people in the Americas, who had no resistance to them. Many [[indigenous|Indigenous]] people were forced to work in mines and on farms.

Spanish was imposed as the language of power, but Indigenous languages did not vanish. Millions of people still speak Quechua in Peru and Bolivia, Guaraní in Paraguay and Nahuatl and Mayan languages in Mexico. Spanish itself borrowed words from them: "chocolate", "tomato" and "avocado" all reached English through Spanish from Nahuatl, [[@aztec-tenochtitlan|the Aztec language]].

Spanish arrived in North America before English did. Spanish explorers founded St. Augustine, in Florida, in 1565, and it is the oldest continuously settled European town in the mainland USA. California, Texas, New Mexico and [[@grand-canyon-state|Arizona]] were once part of Spain's empire and then of [[@mexico|Mexico]], which today has more Spanish speakers than any other country.

Today more than 40 million people in the USA speak Spanish at home, more than any other language except English. In [[@puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]], a US territory, Spanish is the main language. English has borrowed plenty of words from Spanish, including canyon, patio, rodeo, mosquito and tornado.

Spanish sounds different from place to place. In much of Spain, the letter "z" is said like the "th" in "thin". In Latin America, it is said like "s". Mexicans, Argentinians and Cubans each have their own slang and rhythm. A bus is a *camión* in Mexico, a *guagua* in Cuba and a *colectivo* in [[@argentina|Argentina]]. A popcorn seller in Madrid and one in Bogotá might not even use the same word for popcorn.

Even so, a Spanish speaker from Madrid can talk with one from Lima or Los Angeles without much trouble. The Real Academia Española, founded in 1713, works with academies in other Spanish-speaking countries to keep a shared dictionary. The language even has its own letter, ñ, as in *España*.

text: Bengal sits on the world's biggest river [[@deltas|delta]], where the Ganga and [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]] spread into hundreds of channels before reaching the sea. The land is wet and flat, full of rivers, ponds and paddy fields. Rice and fish are everywhere, so they became the heart of Bengali food.

Sweets come from milk. Bengal's sweet-makers became experts at turning milk into soft cheese, called chhena, and then into rosogolla, sandesh and dozens of other sweets. A Bengali meal without fish is unusual, and one without something sweet at the end is almost unthinkable.

Bengal credits the Kolkata sweet-maker Nobin Chandra Das in 1868. Odisha says a version called rasagola was offered at the Jagannath Temple in Puri long before. Both states received official Geographical Indication tags for their own versions.

sec.h: A land of water and fish
sec.t:
In much of West Bengal and Bangladesh, almost every village has a pond. Families raise fish such as rohu and katla in them. Rivers bring prawns, and the coast and the mangrove forests of the [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans]] add crabs and many other fish.

{{story:deltas}}

The most prized fish is the hilsa, or ilish. It lives in the Bay of Bengal but swims up rivers like the Padma and Hooghly during the monsoon to lay eggs. Bengalis cook it in many ways, but a favourite is ilish bhapa, steamed in a paste of mustard seeds.

Bengalis argue cheerfully about whose hilsa is best, from the Padma in Bangladesh or the Ganga in India.

Mustard is the signature flavour. Food is cooked in sharp [[@mustard|mustard oil]], and many fish dishes use a paste of ground mustard seeds that tingles in the nose.

Another key flavour is panch phoron, which means "five spices". It's a mix of whole fenugreek, nigella, cumin, black mustard and fennel seeds. They are fried in hot oil at the start of cooking until they pop, flavouring the whole dish.

A traditional Bengali meal follows an order of tastes. It often starts with something bitter, like shukto, made with bitter gourd and other vegetables. Then come dal, fried vegetables, fish, and sometimes meat. A sweet-sour chutney follows, often made with tomato or raw mango. Finally come sweets and mishti doi, a sweet curd set in clay pots.

Bengal's sweet shops, run by families called moira, are famous across India. Most of their sweets begin with chhena: milk split with an acid like lemon juice into soft curds, a little like fresh [[@cheese-paneer|paneer]].

The rosogolla is a ball of chhena boiled in sugar syrup until it becomes spongy. Bengal credits a Kolkata sweet-maker, Nobin Chandra Das, with creating it in 1868. [[@odisha|Odisha]] says a similar sweet was offered at the Jagannath Temple in Puri long before. After a long dispute, both states received official tags for their own versions.

Sandesh is drier, made by cooking chhena with sugar and pressing it into moulds. In winter, sweet-makers use nolen gur, a [[@jaggery|jaggery]] made from date palm sap.

Food is central to festivals. During [[@durga-puja|Durga Puja]], Kolkata's streets fill with food stalls selling rolls, biryani and sweets. Some families serve bhog, a meal offered at the puja and then shared, with khichuri, vegetables and payesh, a rice pudding.

On Poila Boishakh, the Bengali New Year, families visit sweet shops and eat special lunches. Bengalis in Bangladesh, India and around the world, from London to New Jersey, celebrate with fish, rice and sweets, keeping the old saying alive.

text: Canned food was invented in France in the early 1800s by Nicolas Appert, a confectioner, someone who makes sweets. He found that if he sealed food in glass bottles and heated them in boiling water, the food stayed good for months.

The tin can came soon after. In 1810, an Englishman named Peter Durand patented the idea of using metal containers instead of glass. Within a few years, a factory in London was canning meat and vegetables for the Royal Navy. Ever since, cans have let people carry food across oceans, deserts and even into space.

st.prompt: Nicolas Appert sealed food in bottles and boiled them, and the food stayed good for months. Why did his method work?

options.t: The heat killed microbes, and the seal kept new ones out
Boiling removed all the air's oxygen forever
Glass has special chemicals that preserve food

st.reveal: Appert didn't actually know. Decades later, Louis Pasteur showed that tiny living things called microbes make food rot. Heating kills them, and a sealed lid stops new ones getting in.

Canning destroys some vitamin C and a few other vitamins, but much of the protein, fibre and minerals remains. Canned beans, fish and tomatoes can be healthy foods.

sec.t:
At the end of the 1700s, France was at war, and its armies were often hungrier than their enemies. Soldiers and sailors lived on salted meat and hard biscuits, and many fell ill on long voyages. In 1795, the French government offered a prize of 12,000 francs to anyone who could find a better way to keep food.

Appert spent about fifteen years experimenting in his workshop near Paris. He packed soups, meat, vegetables and fruit into thick glass bottles, corked them tightly, tied the corks with wire and boiled the bottles for hours. In 1810, under Emperor [[@napoleon|Napoleon]], he received the prize and published a book explaining his method.

Appert had no idea why his method worked. Food rots because of [[@microbes-friendly|microbes]], tiny living things like bacteria and moulds that feed on it. In the 1860s, the French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that heating kills many of them, and that food sealed away from the air stays fresh because new microbes can't get in.

Today, factories heat sealed cans to about 121 °C under steam pressure, much hotter than boiling water. The idea is the same as a [[@pressure-cooker|pressure cooker]], which also cooks at higher temperatures by trapping steam. This kills even tough germs, including the one that causes botulism, a rare but dangerous food poisoning.

During the American Civil War in the 1860s, canned food fed soldiers on both sides, and many brought the habit home. Canned soups, beans and fruit became everyday food in the USA. Lighter cans made of steel and [[@aluminium|aluminium]] replaced the old heavy tin-plate, and drink cans arrived in the 1930s.

In India, canned food is less common at home than in the USA, but tins of rasgullas, gulab jamuns and ready-to-eat curries travel with Indian families all over the world. Astronauts, soldiers and mountaineers have long depended on canned and sealed food too.

A can that is badly dented, rusty or bulging should be thrown away, because the seal may be broken and germs may have grown inside. Otherwise, many canned foods last for years.

Empty cans are among the easiest things to [[@recycling|recycle]]. Steel and aluminium can be melted down and made into new cans again and again, without losing quality. A can thrown in a recycling bin today can be back on a shop shelf as a new can within a couple of months.

text: Bread began as a flat, chewy cake of crushed wild grains, cooked on hot stones. The oldest bread crumbs ever found come from a fireplace at a site called Shubayqa in Jordan. They are about 14,400 years old.

The bakers were hunter-gatherers called the Natufians. They had no farms yet. Some scientists think the work of gathering grain for bread may have helped push people toward [[@farming-began|farming]]. Within a few thousand years, wheat was being planted across West Asia, and bread spread with it.

Air whipped in by kneading
Water turning to ice in the dough

st.reveal: Yeast is a tiny fungus. It eats sugars in the flour and gives off carbon dioxide. Gluten, a stretchy net of wheat proteins, traps the bubbles like a balloon.

myth: People only started making bread after they learned to farm.
Crumbs from a hearth in Jordan show that hunter-gatherers ground wild cereals and baked flatbread about 14,400 years ago. That is roughly 4,000 years before farming began in the region.

sec.t:
Wheat was one of the first crops ever farmed, about 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent, an arc of land running through what is now Iraq, Syria and Turkey. Early kinds, called einkorn and emmer, had small seeds and tough husks.

Over generations, farmers kept the plants with the biggest, easiest grains. Wheat reached the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]] in what is now Pakistan and India by about 5,000 years ago. Today India is the second biggest wheat grower in the world, after [[@china-today|China]], and much of it comes from Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]].

Mix wheat flour with water and two proteins join up into gluten. Gluten makes dough stretchy, a bit like [[@chewing-gum|chewing gum]]. Knead it and the strands line up into a strong net.

Barley, rice and millet have little or no gluten, so they make flatter breads. That is why bajra and jowar rotis are rolled thicker and patted out by hand. A few people cannot eat gluten at all, because their bodies react badly to it. This is called coeliac disease, and doctors can test for it. This is why wheat became the grain of choice for puffy loaves, and why a [[@roti-chapati|roti]] made from wheat atta can blow up like a balloon.

Bread took different shapes around the world. Clay ovens like the tandoor, sunk into the ground, baked naan on their hot walls. The Portuguese brought yeast-raised loaves to Goa in the 16th century, which is where the soft pav of Mumbai's vada pav comes from.

In 1928, a bakery in Chillicothe, Missouri, sold the first loaves cut by Otto Rohwedder's slicing machine. [[@bread-factory|Sliced bread]] caught on so fast that Americans still call a new idea "the best thing since sliced bread".

Sourdough is bread raised by a "starter", a jar of flour paste full of wild yeast and bacteria that bakers keep feeding for years. It is how most bread was made before factory yeast went on sale in the 1800s. Home bakers in many countries took it up again during the COVID-19 lockdowns of 2020, when shops ran short of packets of yeast.
